'''Daniel S. Akerib''' (born June 19, 1962) is an American [[particle physicist]] and [[astrophysicist]]. He was elected in 2008 a [[Fellows of the American Physical Society|fellow]] of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).<ref name=APS>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2008&unit_id=&institution=Case+Western+Reserve+University}} (search on year=2008 and institution=Case Western Reserve University)</ref>

==Biography==
Akerib graduated in 1984 with an A.B. from the [[University of Chicago]] and in 1990 with a Ph.D. in physics from [[Princeton University]].<ref name=Stanford>{{cite web|url=https://physics.stanford.edu/people/daniel-akerib|title=Daniel Akerib|website=Physics Department, Stanford University}}</ref> ''A search for the rare decay [[kaon|{{math|K}}]]<sup>+</sup> → [[pion|{{pi}}]]<sup>+ </sup>{{ math|[[neutrino|ν]][[antineutrino|{{overline|ν}}]]}}'' is the title of his Ph.D. thesis (which finds experimental limits for a particular type of rare decay involving [[kaon]]s).<ref>{{cite journal|title=A search for rare decay K sup + yields. pi. sup +. nu. nu. (abstract of D. S. Akerib's doctoral thesis)|website=Office of Scientifica and Technical Information, U.S. Department of Energy (osti.gov)|year=1991|osti=5260890 |url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/5260890-search-rare-decay-sup-yields-pi-sup-nu-nu |last1=Akerib |first1=D. S. }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=A search for the rare decay K<sup>+</sup> --> π<sup>+</sup>vv̄ / Daniel S. Akerib|year=1991|website=Catalog, Princeton University Library|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/996124733506421}}</ref> As a postdoc he did research from 1990 to 1992 at [[California Institute of Technology]] and from 1993 to 1996 at [[UC Berkeley]]'s Center for Particle Astrophysics<ref name=Stanford/> (which was started in 1989 with funding from the [[National Science Foundation]]).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Gwynne, Peter|title=US Science: New centers established|journal=Physics World|volume=2|issue=2|page=10|year=1989|doi=10.1088/2058-7058/2/2/8}}</ref> In the physics department of [[Case Western Reserve University]], he was from 1995 to 2001 an assistant professor, from 2001 to 2004 an associate professor, and from 2004 to 2014 a full professor. He also chaired the department from 2007 to 2010.<ref name=Stanford/> Akerib has been a professor of particle physics and astrophysics at [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory]] since 2014, with a courtesy full-time professorship in [[Stanford University]]'s physics department.<ref name=Stanford/>

Akerib was involved for about two years (from 2019 to 2020) in the [[Cosmic microwave background|CMB]]-Stage 4 (CMB-S4) experiment to detect [[primordial gravitational wave]]s and to gather data about the [[Timeline of the early universe|early universe]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Daniel Akerib|website=Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology (KIPAC)|url=https://kipac.stanford.edu/people/daniel-akerib}}</ref> but is no longer involved.

At Case Western Reserve University from 2008 to 2014, he worked with Thomas A. Shutt on the [[Large Underground Xenon]] (LUX) experiment to detect dark matter particles. In 2014 both were appointed to professorships at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and Stanford University.<ref>{{cite web|website=SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|date=July 1, 2014|url=https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2014-07-01-noted-dark-matter-experts-daniel-akerib-and-thomas-shutt-join-slac-faculty.aspx|title=Noted Dark Matter Experts Daniel Akerib and Thomas Shutt Join SLAC Faculty }}</ref> The two became the leaders of the SLAC establishment of a Liquid Nobles Test Platform.<ref name=Stanford/><ref>{{cite web|title=Noble liquid detector R&D with the LZ System Test platform at SLAC|author=Stifter, Kelly|date=December 10, 2018|website=LZ Collaboration, Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (lz.lbl.gov)|url=https://lz.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2019/09/CPAD-2018-w_-LZ-Slide-Template-Blue.pdf}}</ref> Their group "specializes in detector development, xenon purification, and simulations".<ref name=Stanford/>

Akerib's 2008 APS fellowship citation is for "significant contributions to direct Dark Matter detection experiments, in particular for his work on the [[Cryogenic Dark Matter Search|CDMS]] experiment."<ref name=APS/>

Since the 1990s he has done research on the search for [[Weakly interacting massive particle|WIMP]]s, beginning with the [[Cryogenic Dark Matter Search]] and in recent years with the [[Large Underground Xenon experiment]] and the [[LZ experiment|LUX-ZEPLIN Experiment]]. He now works on expanding and improving time projection chambers to improve sensitivity for possible detection of WIMPs. Such chambers use liquid [[xenon]] as a target medium.<ref name=Stanford/>

<!--Personal life-->
On May 31, 1992, in [[Lodi, New York]], he married Chantal Christ.<ref>{{cite news|title=Wedding Akerib - Christ |newspaper=Daily Press (DailyPress.com)|date=June 14, 1992|url=https://www.dailypress.com/news/dp-xpm-19920614-1992-06-14-9206150271-story.html}}</ref>
